summary: Discusses how a company's data classification policy can be mapped onto the S/MIME security label. It gives worked examples drawn from the policies of three real companies.

plainLanguage.summary: Companies stamp papers like secret or public. This shows how to put the same stamps on secure email.

how do companies control who can read classified email

how do i implement company security policy in email
subtitle: How to mark secure email with company classification levels

tldr.problem: Companies classify information (secret, confidential, public) and need to enforce these classifications on email. How can the S/MIME security label mechanism carry this information?
tldr.mechanism: Companies define their classification policies and map them to the ESSSecurityLabel syntax defined in RFC 2634, using classification values, privacy marks, and security categories that match their business rules.
tldr.outcome: Three real companies (Amoco, Caterpillar, Whirlpool) provided their policies as worked examples, showing how different industries can implement access control on secure email while respecting their own business needs.

today: RFC 3114 is an Informational RFC published in May 2002 documenting how company security policies can be implemented using the S/MIME security label mechanism. It has not been updated or obsoleted. The document remains a reference for organizations implementing classification-based access control in email systems.

sections.title: Information Classification Policies
sections.content:
Organizations treat information as an asset and need to protect it appropriately based on its value. An information classification policy defines how information should be protected based on its type. Some information, such as research plans, marketing strategies, or manufacturing specifications, provides competitive advantage and requires strong protection. Other information, such as internal organization charts or employee lists, may require little protection.

A corporate classification policy guides employees on how to classify information and how to handle it based on its classification and state (electronic, on paper, in transit, or stored). The S/MIME security label provides a mechanism to carry this classification information in secure email and to enable access control systems to enforce the policy automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: Different information needs different levels of protection. The company decides which things are secret, which are just for inside the company, and which are public. The security label attaches that decision to the email so the email system can treat it the right way.

sections.title: Security Labels and Access Control
sections.content:
An S/MIME security label is a set of signed attributes that can be included in a SignedData object. It carries information about the sensitivity of the message content. The label may be included in the inner signature (for plaintext access control), the outer signature (for encrypted message access control), or both in a triple-wrapped message.

Access control can be rule-based (algorithmically expressed policies), identity-based (explicit lists of who can access what), rank-based (hierarchical organizational positions), or role-based (job functions such as Database Administrator). The security label supports all of these by conveying the classification to the email system, which then compares it with the recipient's authorizations. A recipient's authorizations are carried in clearance attributes, which can be stored in X.509 certificates or Attribute Certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: The label on the email tells the system how secret it is. The system checks your clearance (your job allows you to see this level of secret) and decides whether to let you read it.

sections.title: Real Company Examples
sections.content:
Amoco classifies information on two independent axes: confidentiality (General, Confidential, Highly Confidential) and integrity (Minimum, Medium, Maximum). It also defines availability classifications (Critical) for time-sensitive information. This three-dimensional approach allows the same document to be marked for different types of protection.

Caterpillar uses a single confidentiality hierarchy of four levels: Public, Green (provides business advantage), Yellow (moderate competitive advantage), and Red (significant competitive advantage causing severe damage if disclosed). Whirlpool uses three confidentiality levels: Public (official public release), Internal (proprietary information), and Confidential (information whose disclosure would harm the company). Whirlpool also allows additional caveats such as "Make No Copies" or "Attorney-Client Privileged Document" to be added to classify sensitive information further.
sections.plainLanguage: Amoco has three secret levels and separates rules for protecting information from being read versus being changed. Caterpillar has four levels based on how much damage leaking would do. Whirlpool has three levels and adds extra warnings like "do not copy this" when needed.

sections.title: Technical Implementation
sections.content:
The ESSSecurityLabel syntax defined in RFC 2634 consists of a security policy identifier, security classification value, optional privacy mark, and optional security categories. Each company defines its own object identifier for its security policy to distinguish its rules from others.

Security classification values are hierarchical integers. For example, Amoco uses 6 (general), 7 (confidential), and 8 (highly confidential). Security categories provide additional granularity for sensitive information. A company might define categories like "Legal Only" or "Project Vallor" to restrict access to specific organizational units or projects. Clearance attributes carried in certificates specify what classifications and categories a user is authorized to access. Access control is granted only if the recipient's clearance covers every classification value and category in the message's label.
sections.plainLanguage: Each company has a number for each level (6, 7, 8, etc.). The email tells what number it is. Your clearance says what numbers you are allowed to see. If your number is not high enough or does not match the extra categories, you cannot read it.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
A critical implementation issue is mapping security label values to human-readable text. The values may be encoded in non-human-readable form, and companies may want to update their classifications regularly. Hard-coding mappings into applications is discouraged. Using a Security Policy Information File (SPIF), a signed object that contains domain-specific policy information, allows enterprises to manage classification display strings and policy information centrally without updating applications.

Another practical issue is obtaining recipient certificates when sending signed-only messages. Normally, recipient certificates are needed only for encrypted messages, but to check the recipient's clearance, the sender's application needs the recipient's certificate even for signed-only messages with a security label. Applications must support retrieving certificates for this purpose. All security considerations from RFC 2630 (Cryptographic Message Syntax) and RFC 2634 (Enhanced Security Services) apply to implementations using these procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The system needs to know what label number 8 means in English. The company maintains a file that shows which text to display for each number. If you want to let someone read a message, your email system needs to get their clearance information from their certificate first.
